title: Physiological changes associated with the pre-event taper in athletes
authors: Mujika I, Padilla S, Pyne D, Busso T
population: Athletes across sports (review of physiological taper studies)
findings: Maximal oxygen uptake may increase but is not a necessary prerequisite for taper-induced performance gains; resting, maximal and submaximal heart rates do not change unless athletes show clear signs of overreaching before the taper.

Possible haematological changes include increased blood and red cell volume, haemoglobin, haematocrit and reticulocytes; muscle glycogen concentration increases progressively; reduced blood creatine kinase suggests recovery from muscle damage.
Neuromuscular strength and power usually increase markedly; psychological changes include reduced total mood disturbance, reduced perception of effort and improved sleep quality.

Mathematical models indicate taper effects result from restoration of impaired capacities (fatigue and adaptation model) and the capacity to respond to training during the taper (variable dose-response model).
limitations: Narrative review; heterogeneous populations and designs; physiological changes are correlated with, not shown to cause, performance gains.
implications: Resting HR is not expected to change in healthy tapering athletes, so a rise in resting HR is worth a caution flag (engine inference, not a stated finding).
Subjective readiness, mood and sleep are expected to improve across the taper; absence of improvement is a reasonable check item (inference).
No numeric taper parameter is justified from this review alone.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Sports Med 2004). The abstract does not mention HRV; the researcher's HRV-fall flag was an inference and is contradicted in nuance by hug-2014 (post-exercise RMSSD fell during taper), so HRV wording was removed.
